title: Sorting Room Showdown
tagline: Correct the last postal blunder before the whole route collapses.
premise: The mail has become a chain of mistakes, and two sorters must correct it one error at a time. On every turn, name a standing postal item or instruction that fixes the one before it; the Judge rules whether the correction really works.

seed_pool.opening_token: a letter addressed only to that blue house near the big tree
a parcel with no return address
a stamp stuck to the wrong corner

tests: A stranger pictures the postal item and the mistake at once. Nothing abstract, nothing that needs a clerk's private code.
A non-player names a plain postal correction within five seconds. Say what that correction is.
It belongs in the sorting room. It can be stamped, sorted, labeled, sealed, weighed, returned, rerouted, or delivered.
It makes a stranger want to answer. A thing with a little postal drama, like a furious notice or a parcel nobody ordered.
Two to five everyday words a twelve-year-old knows. No brand names, proper nouns, office jargon, or quotation marks inside the card.

move_constraints.example: I am a postcode; I force this letter onto the right street.
move_constraints.hint: Name the postal thing, then name the correction it performs.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How directly and completely your postal item corrects the exact mistake in the item before it.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no correction or only a restatement; 1 = claims to help but leaves the error untouched; 2 = plausible correction with a gap or disputed connection; 3 = clear postal fix that resolves the mistake; 4 = exact, decisive correction that leaves the error nowhere to go (rare).

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How plainly a stranger can picture the item, its postal purpose, and the correction happening.
rubric.anchors: 0 = contradictory or unreadable; 1 = requires specialist postal knowledge; 2 = understandable but cluttered or vague; 3 = concrete and easy to follow; 4 = crisp, vivid, and instantly legible (rare). Length never wins by itself: every extra clause must clarify the correction.

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: How freshly the move changes postal function rather than repeating the same tool, route, or correction.
rubric.anchors: 0 = stock answer, duplicate, or the same correction as the previous move; 2 = a reasonable change of postal angle; 4 = a surprising but plain correction from a new corner of the mail system (rare). Fancy wording is not novelty, and obscure postal trivia earns nothing.

criterion.description: A move OVERCOMES the standing postal item if it directly corrects, separates, reroutes, seals, labels, returns, or otherwise makes that item's mistake impossible. The correction must act on the standing item, not merely hide it, ignore it, outlast it, or make the same mistake larger.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, discussing the game, or citing rules is itself a failed postal item and loses the turn.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no previous move: judge it against the opening card and ask whether it directly corrects that opening mistake.
A larger, faster, or more expensive version of the standing postal item is not a correction. A second wrong address after a first wrong address is the same error wearing a fresh uniform.
Becoming the opening item itself, or making only a cosmetic change to it, is a duplicate and fails.
The move must act on the standing postal item. A postcard that simply waits for a lost parcel, or a mailbox that ignores an unreadable address, is dodging rather than correcting.

The mechanism must be literal and watchable. A label can identify, a stamp can show postage, a seal can close an envelope, and a sorter can send mail to another route. A promise, metaphor, or bureaucratic slogan is not a mechanism.
Merely hiding, ignoring, outlasting, or enlarging the same mistake fails. Putting a bad address in a bigger envelope does not repair the address.
A correction that works only by assuming an unstated clerk, machine, tracking system, or miracle fails unless the move itself clearly supplies that postal action.
The correction must match the actual mistake. A return label can fix an undeliverable parcel, but it does not by itself repair a stamp stuck to the wrong corner.

voice_rules: One sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
Speak like a velvet curtained postal tribunal. Make the correction sound momentous, even when it is a label.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger reading only the two forms must see exactly how the winner corrected the loser.
Name both postal forms, or their plain stand ins. A headline that could fit any parcel is a dead letter.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Postmaster refuses.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Mock the doomed postal item and its magnificent failure. A roast level jab at the player is allowed, but never target identity, body, family, intelligence, or spelling.
Plain spoken English with theatrical grandeur. No fake Latin, no poetry, no antique fog, no thesaurus parade.
On a refusal caused by a gate failure, the headline refuses the move and asks for another. It never declares a winner.
The coaching line names one postal form that would have worked. It ends on a concrete action or postal fact, never a mood or verdict.
good_headlines: The blue house was a terrible address, so the postcode summons the letter to the correct street.
The parcel arrived without a return address, and the sender form gives its escape route a name.
The forwarding label drags the wrong street back into the royal postal procession.
A bigger stamp is still lost in the corner. Bring a label that moves the postage.
The locked mailbox buries the mystery instead of solving it. Bring a return address.
The seal closes the envelope, and at last the letter stops leaking its secrets onto the sorting floor.
The parcel had no route, but the sorting code has now handed it a destination.
The stamp wore the wrong corner like a crown. A placement label would put it where the machines look.
The letter is not corrected by being ignored. Give it a postcode and send it down a real street.
The return label wins the parcel's grand escape, while the missing address is finally shown the door.

bad_headlines.why: opens with a status word and gives no postal mechanism

bad_headlines.text: The Grand Postmaster refuses, your parcel has offended the crown.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase, names the host, and attacks the player instead of explaining the correction

bad_headlines.text: Move refused, excellent effort from the genius who mailed a blank box.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and uses a personal insult without naming the failed mechanism

bad_headlines.text: The label defeats the envelope with majestic administrative force.
bad_headlines.why: grand language replaces the literal correction

bad_headlines.text: A larger stamp is more powerful, therefore it wins.
bad_headlines.why: mere amplification is treated as correction

bad_headlines.text: The parcel survives its address crisis through patience and destiny.
bad_headlines.why: survival and mood are not a postal action

bad_headlines.text: Your move is stupid and the sorting room is embarrassed.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player and gives no concrete reason

bad_headlines.text: The envelope, magnificent and sorrowful, seeks the moonlit route of fate.
The stamp wins, conquers, triumphs, and utterly dominates the corner.
bad_headlines.why: repeats verdict words without showing what the stamp corrects

bad_headlines.text: Perhaps the box could maybe be returned if someone happened to notice.
bad_headlines.why: hedges instead of making a clear ruling

rules: Correct the postal mistake in front of you. Do not merely hide it or become it.
Name your postal thing and its correction: I am a zip code; I force this address onto the right street.
The Judge rules on the postal idea, never the spelling.
One form that fails to correct the standing mistake ends the sorting chain.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next correction while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing in the tray. Name a postal correction.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. A correction, not a filing cabinet.
validation_messages.duplicate: That postal form already crossed this match. Send something new.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Correct {standing_form}. Do not hide it, enlarge it, or repeat its mistake.

judge_out_text: The judge has left the sorting room. Nobody reroutes anything until they return. {standing_form} still stands. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two postal sorters trying to keep the mail system alive.
Always name a postal thing and the direct correction it performs.
Good: "I am a postcode; I force this letter onto the right street."
Good: "I am a return label; I send this undeliverable parcel back to its sender."
Bad: "I am a label, majestic and important" because it names no correction.
Bad: "I am a bigger envelope" because size does not repair the mistake.
Bad: "I am patience" because a mood is not postal machinery.
Talk like a person across a sorting table, not a poet or a bureaucrat hiding behind fog.
Use plain things anyone can picture: stamps, labels, envelopes, bins, routes, forms, scales, seals, mailbags, and delivery vans.
Your move must act directly on the standing postal item. Correct it, separate it, reroute it, seal it, label it, return it, or make its mistake impossible.
Do not merely hide it, ignore it, wait it out, or make the same error larger.
Hop domains inside the postal world: a counter, a sorting belt, a rural route, a return desk, a customs table, a mailbox.
Never reuse a form or an attribute from this match.
You are not performing for a crowd and you are not joking. You are trying to keep the mail moving.
default_move: I am a sorting label; I send this item to the right tray.
